text: A QuantumCircuit with no gates on it is just an empty container. Gates are what actually do something — operations that rotate and transform the quantum state of each qubit. Qiskit gives every common single-qubit gate a short method you call directly on the circuit.

X, Y, and Z are the three Pauli gates — fixed, self-inverse operations with no adjustable parameter. X flips the bit, Z flips the phase of |1>. H is the workhorse of quantum computing: applied to |0>, it produces an equal superposition, the starting point for almost every interesting algorithm. S and T are smaller phase rotations used once you need fine-grained phase control.

Unlike the fixed gates, the rotation gates RX, RY, and RZ take an explicit angle in radians, letting you rotate a qubit's state by any amount you choose. These are the gates that make variational algorithms possible, in Chapter 6: you treat the angle as a tunable parameter and let an optimizer search over it.

For small circuits, you don't need thousands of shots to know what a circuit produces — you can ask Qiskit for the exact mathematical statevector directly, with Statevector of qc. This gives the complex amplitude for every basis state, with no sampling noise involved at all.

Starting from |0>, qc.h(0) produces 0.7071068 and 0.7071068, both real and equal — the famous plus state, with P(0)=0.5 and P(1)=0.5. qc.rx of pi over 2 on qubit 0 produces 0.7071068 and negative 0.7071068 times i — an imaginary second amplitude. The measurement probabilities work out the same, because probability only depends on squared magnitude. But the states are not identical: RX introduced a relative phase that H never does, invisible to a single measurement right now, but something downstream operations are sensitive to.

Next lesson crosses back into the classical world: how a classical register receives a measurement, and why that measurement is a one-way, irreversible collapse of superposition — not a side-effect-free read.
